note: Kapitel 4, Teil 2 – Erkundung im Lokdepot Karsk (Alexei: Kohlenbansen am Montagmorgen, Schauseite und Bahnsteig 1 am Dienstagabend) und in Berlin (Konrad: Korridorbahnsteig K am Ostbahnhof, Hof der Kolonnenstraße 14), die Aufgaben „Ein Paket über die Linie“ und „Ein Korb für Frau Grabowski“, die Minispiele „Die Drehscheibe“ und „Die Gepäckwaage“. Funde in der Stimme dessen, der sie erreichen kann. Daten: data/explore/c4p2_karsk.json, c4p2_berlin.json; Karten zur realen Geschichte: de_history_c4p2.json.

strings.char.grabowski.name: Frau Grabowski
strings.explore.karsk.depot.duty_board.title: Seven names
strings.explore.karsk.depot.duty_board.text: Irina’s duty roster on the plank wall: seven drivers, after each name the passport number and the propiska – barrack 4, Garden Street 9, depot hostel. For the corridor each needs a second stamp in his passport. After Saizew, Irina has written ‘sick’ in red pencil, the lead still fresh. Yesterday Saizew was sitting in the engine shed playing cards, fit as a fiddle. Irina protects her people as best she can: with paper.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.canteen_radio.title: Grain and a waltz
strings.explore.karsk.depot.canteen_radio.text: Through the canteen hatch a pot of kasha is steaming. The radio on the windowsill reads out figures: grain for the corridor, wagons heading west, plan fulfilment one hundred and four per cent. Then a waltz. For the figures the cook turns it down, for the waltz up. I wonder who in Karsk eats the hundred and four per cent.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.water_crane.title: The water crane
strings.explore.karsk.depot.water_crane.text: The water crane is wrapped in straw and sacking; at the bottom, coke glows in a bucket so the pipe won’t burst. Someone has patched the joint with wire, someone else wrapped the wire in rags, a third wrapped the rags in wire. Three winters of repairs on top of each other. Here nothing lasts long, but everything holds.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.kolonne_shoes.title: Shoes from Veltrava
strings.explore.karsk.depot.kolonne_shoes.text: By the ramp, shoes stand in a row: women’s strapped shoes, men’s shoes with stitched soles, split by the coal dust. Beside them the issued felt boots, too big, stuffed with straw. They came in shoes made for Veltrava pavements. For shovelling you take them off and set them neatly side by side, as if you’ll need them again soon.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.lena_mitten.title: A mitten
strings.explore.karsk.depot.lena_mitten.text: Low down on a post of the coal bunker, fixed with a horseshoe nail: a child’s mitten of grey wool. Embroidered on the cuff in Latin letters: ‘Lena’. Someone nailed it up so it can be seen while shovelling, every time you bend down. I leave it hanging.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.chat_maria.title: Maria Gorelowa
strings.explore.karsk.depot.chat_maria.text: Maria sews gloves for the column, and for the young guard too. I told her where Children’s Home Number Two stands and which windows face the yard. That was all I had.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.chat_maria.l1: The needle on your collar. They let you keep it?
strings.explore.karsk.depot.chat_maria.l2: A needle isn’t on any list. I sew gloves for the column. For the guard too.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.chat_maria.l4: He’s nineteen. His mother sent him off with gloves she can’t sew. You can tell.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.chat_maria.l5: Children’s Home Number Two is behind the water tower. Three storeys; the little ones’ windows face the yard.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.chat_maria.l6: On Sundays we’re not allowed into town. But from the coal bunker you can see the water tower.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.chat_maria.l7: In the evenings there’s a light on there. On the second floor.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.chat_maria.l8: Then now I know where to look in the evenings. Go, Engineer. He’s coming with the tea.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.ash_pit_dog.title: The Inspector
strings.explore.karsk.depot.ash_pit_dog.text: In the warmth of the ash pit a dog is sleeping, sooty, with one ear that always stands up. The firemen call him ‘Inspector’ because every morning he walks along all the engines and then lies down. In the break he rests his head on the felt boots of the woman in the green headscarf. He doesn’t care which wagon anyone came in.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.barrel_fire.title: The fire in the drum
strings.explore.karsk.depot.barrel_fire.text: The guard at the drum tells me he is nineteen and from Kursk before I ask. He looks into the fire and not at the column, as if he had been ordered to. On the rim of the drum two darned women’s gloves lie drying, far too thin for Karsk. When nobody is looking, he turns them over. I don’t look.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.banner_back.title: The back side
strings.explore.karsk.depot.banner_back.text: Since last night there have been posts here, and the first length of tarpaulin is already hanging, for Tuesday. From behind it is a patchwork: sacking, a groundsheet, a potato sack with a stamp. In front they are painting letters; here the red paint shows through, back to front. Low down on a board, a train in chalk, by a child’s hand: engine, three wagons, a curl of smoke, and at every window a stroke that is meant to be a face.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.tarpaulin_front.text: From the front, the tarpaulin is a banner in the floodlights: ВОССТАНОВИМ ВМЕСТЕ, ‘Together we rebuild’, red on white. Bottom left, a tear a hand’s breadth wide. Behind it, very close, a shovel handle and a hand that keeps still, because someone at the front is taking photographs. The column hears every word from here. We hear nothing from them.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.signal_scratch.title: А. М., 1949
strings.explore.karsk.depot.signal_scratch.text: Low down on the signal mast, a hand’s breadth above the ballast, scratched into the rust: ‘А. М. 1949’. We apprentices put up the mast in the autumn of forty-nine. I was fourteen and bent down so the foreman wouldn’t see. Today a painter painted the mast for the Swede, from the top down to a hand’s breadth above the ballast. Nobody looks that far down.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.parcel_wire.title: Signal wire
strings.explore.karsk.depot.parcel_wire.text: At the foot of the signal lies the coil of signal wire from my repair in January, galvanised and stiff with cold. I cut off an arm’s length and wind it round my fist. In January this wire pulled a signal to green. Today it is to hold a parcel together all the way to Veltrava.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.model_engine.title: The model engine
strings.explore.karsk.depot.model_engine.text: The model engine gleams like a samovar: red bows on the handrail, a wreath on the smokebox door, the tyres whitened with chalk. A cleaner rubbed at it for three days, with sand, oil and rags from old uniforms. The brass plate says 1939. Since the war it hasn’t run a single kilometre. For the photo it only has to stand.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.minder.title: The press minder
strings.explore.karsk.depot.minder.text: The press minder hasn’t slept since Sunday. He counts glasses, flags and sentences, and tells the Swede twelve times a day: write ‘reconstruction’. A tarpaulin he does not see.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.minder.l1: Engineer Morozov, the one with the signal. Smile later. But not too much, it looks ordered.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.minder.l2: You look as if you haven’t slept.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.minder.l3: Not since Sunday. I count glasses, flags and sentences. The Swede writes faster than I can read.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.minder.l4: And what is he supposed to write?
strings.explore.karsk.depot.minder.l5: Write: reconstruction. I tell him that twelve times a day. He nods every time.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.minder.l6: And if he writes something else?
strings.explore.karsk.depot.minder.l7: Then I’m the second to read it. The first sits in Moscow and writes me a letter afterwards.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.minder.l9: What tarpaulin, Engineer? I see a banner.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.brass_band.title: The band
strings.explore.karsk.depot.brass_band.text: The railwaymen’s band on its plank platform: two trumpets, a horn, a drum, a tuba. The tuba is played by Grigori, Irina’s husband, red in the face with cold and earnestness. For a week they rehearsed the March of the Agreement, evenings in the engine shed, and Irina held her ears. The firemen’s children sit on the edge of the platform and march along sitting down.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.press_buffet.title: Caviar and kasha
strings.explore.karsk.depot.press_buffet.text: White tablecloth, tea glasses in silver holders, bread with caviar, red and black, neatly laid in a circle. Twelve place settings for two guests: empty places, says the minder, look like shortage in photos. Behind the curtain stands the pot of kasha for the band. What the column eats is on no table.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.turntable.title: The turntable
strings.explore.karsk.depot.turntable.text: The Kukushka stands in stall 7, the door shut. Grigori, who usually works the turntable, is playing the tuba today, so I stopped the bridge myself, to within two fingers’ breadth, as he showed me when I was an apprentice. First the column behind the tarpaulin, now the engine behind the door. Whatever is dirty is taken out of the picture.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.chat_lev.title: Lev under the lamp
strings.explore.karsk.depot.chat_lev.text: Lev has seen papers from Brest, from 1940, with stamps across the border. The papers are in the archive; the people are not. In a few minutes the card must go back into the box.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.chat_lev.l1: Twenty-five minutes left. Then it’s back in the box, and the stamp is half again.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.chat_lev.l2: Have you ever seen anything like it? A stamp across two countries?
strings.explore.karsk.depot.chat_lev.l3: Nineteen forty, papers from Brest. The stamps went across the border then too. And the people with them.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.chat_lev.l5: The papers are in the archive. The people aren’t.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.chat_lev.l6: Lev. If something goes wrong tonight …
strings.explore.karsk.depot.chat_lev.l7: Then you keep counting, Morozov. Someone has to count. Go, the Swede is waiting at the train.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.parcel_scale.title: Five kilos six hundred
strings.explore.karsk.depot.parcel_scale.text: On the sack scale in the sand shed the old woman’s parcel weighs five kilos six hundred. Five may cross the Line, and at Kordon-17 they weigh again. I undo the string: wool socks, a piece of bacon, dried apples and right at the bottom a jar of honey, wrapped in newspaper. Six hundred grams. Exactly what is too much.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.two_clocks.title: Two clocks
strings.explore.karsk.depot.two_clocks.text: Above the gate to platform 1 hang two clocks. The big one shows Karsk time, ten past seven. The small one beside it has an enamel sign, ‘Corridor time’, and is two hours behind. The trains of the Agreement run by it, the special run tonight too: at Kordon-17 at 23:40 corridor time, twenty to two by ours. Two clocks, one train.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.platform_families.te: By the sleeping car stand families who are not travelling. A woman holds out her pass to a militiaman, two stamps, two languages; he reads it twice, once for each. A man hands a passenger a small parcel through the window; a child sits on the suitcase eating a pirozhok. Farewell with a stamp. Here even the waving is regulated.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.parcel_ask.title: A parcel for Kolja
strings.explore.karsk.depot.parcel_ask.text: An old woman on platform 1 wants to send her son in Veltrava a parcel. The post office sent it back: overweight. There is a scale in the sand shed.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.parcel_ask.l1: Sonny, you’re from the depot, aren’t you? Does that train go over the Line?
strings.explore.karsk.depot.parcel_ask.l2: Over Kordon-17, westward. At ten past eight.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.parcel_ask.l3: My Kolja’s been in Veltrava since the war. Stoker for the Commission. Since the Agreement I’m allowed to send him things.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.parcel_ask.l5: The post sent it back, ‘overweight’. I weighed it with my hand, and my hand said: that’ll do.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.parcel_ask.l6: There’s a scale in the sand shed. Give it here.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.parcel_ask.l7: Careful, sonny. There’s something at the bottom that breaks.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.parcel_letter.title: A letter instead of honey
strings.explore.karsk.depot.parcel_letter.text: The honey stays in Karsk. Instead there is a letter in the parcel: ‘Kolja, the honey is waiting for you. Come and fetch it.’ I didn’t tell her what happens at the coal bunker to those who come back.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.parcel_letter.l1: Five kilos six hundred. The jar of honey is too much.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.parcel_letter.l2: Lime-blossom honey, from my garden. As a boy he ate it out of the jar with his finger.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.parcel_letter.l3: Write and tell him it’s there. A letter weighs twenty grams.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.parcel_letter.l4: Give me the pencil. ‘Kolja, the honey is waiting for you. Come and fetch it.’ There. I can’t write more than that.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.parcel_letter.l6: Oh, the string’s broken. Everything breaks when you open it twice.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.parcel_conductor.tex: The conductor takes the parcel as a present for his nephew Kolja. The old woman doesn’t wave, as he told her. She holds her hand in front of her mouth, the way you do when you mustn’t laugh.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.parcel_conductor.l1: The train doesn’t take parcels, comrade. That’s what the post is for.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.parcel_conductor.l2: The post sent it back. Now it weighs five kilos, weighed on the depot scale. For a stoker in Veltrava.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.parcel_conductor.l3: At Kordon-17 they weigh everything twice. Once German, once Russian.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.parcel_conductor.l4: It weighs the same both times.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.parcel_conductor.l5: Then from now on it’s a present for my nephew. What’s his name?
strings.explore.karsk.depot.parcel_conductor.l6: Kolja. Stoker for the Commission in Veltrava.
strings.explore.karsk.depot.parcel_conductor.l7: My nephew Kolja. At Kordon-17 it goes on the train to Veltrava. And tell his mother: no waving. Waving gets noticed.
strings.task.karsk.parcel.title: A parcel across the Line
strings.task.karsk.parcel.summary: An old woman on platform 1 wants to send her son in Veltrava a parcel. The post office sent it back: overweight.
strings.task.karsk.parcel.hint.ask: Talk to the old woman on platform 1 who is clutching a parcel.
strings.task.karsk.parcel.hint.scale: Weigh the parcel on the sack scale in the sand-drying shed.
strings.task.karsk.parcel.hint.letter: Take the parcel back to the old woman. Six hundred grams are too much.
strings.task.karsk.parcel.hint.wire: The string has broken. At the foot of your signal there’s still signal wire from January.
strings.task.karsk.parcel.hint.conductor: Give the parcel to the conductor at the sleeping car.
strings.explore.berlin.ost.liaison_booth.title: One table, two states
strings.explore.berlin.ost.liaison_booth.text: At the barrier to platform K, a glass booth with two chairs. On the left a Soviet liaison officer, a tea glass in a tin holder in front of him. On the right a German railway policeman with a stamp pad and a ruler. They share a table, a lamp and a list, and neither looks at the other. The Agreement on one square metre. I have drawn booths like this, scale one to fifty.
strings.explore.berlin.ost.luggage_scale.title: The luggage scale
strings.explore.berlin.ost.luggage_scale.text: The suitcase for the grandmother in Karsk now weighs nineteen kilos eight hundred, the parcel three kilos eight hundred. Together exactly as much as before, only in a form the corridor allows. The official stamped both without looking up. All day long I do nothing else: I put things into a form that gets through.
strings.explore.berlin.ost.corridor_permit.title: Two stamps
strings.explore.berlin.ost.corridor_permit.text: At the buffet a family, the boy asleep on the suitcase. The mother shows me her pass as if I were the inspection: Karsk, once a year, to her mother. Two stamps, two languages, a signature in each. She came to Berlin in forty-two, ‘for work’, she says, looking at the pass as she says it. It is in cellophane. If you travel only once a year, you don’t want it creased.
strings.explore.berlin.ost.chat_marta.title: Coffee at the buffet
strings.explore.berlin.ost.chat_marta.text: Marta is only holding on to her coffee. Ilse asked about her mother, and whether she has a suitcase. Tomorrow evening Marta will bring her to Kolonnenstraße.
strings.explore.berlin.ost.chat_marta.l1: Are you still drinking that coffee?
strings.explore.berlin.ost.chat_marta.l2: Nobody here drinks it. It’s for holding on to.
strings.explore.berlin.ost.chat_marta.l4: She asked about her mother. I said she’s away travelling. So she asked: with a suitcase?
strings.explore.berlin.ost.chat_marta.l6: I said yes. People who get taken away don’t pack a suitcase. She needn’t know that yet.
strings.explore.berlin.ost.chat_marta.l7: Tomorrow evening, Kolonnenstraße fourteen. Side wing, third floor.
strings.explore.berlin.ost.chat_marta.l8: I know where teachers live. Always wherever it’s coldest.
strings.explore.berlin.ost.kiosk.title: Sold out
strings.explore.berlin.ost.kiosk.text: At the kiosk, the day’s papers, all with the same headline in different typefaces: ‘A Winter of Peace’. Below it the plan figures, below that the weather. On a hook, a little card: ‘Swedish press – sold out’. The gentleman next to me is reading the same page as before. I buy a paper I won’t read. Two of you are less conspicuous.
strings.explore.berlin.ost.green_car.title: The green wagon
strings.explore.berlin.ost.green_car.text: On the next track the green wagon without windows, its hatches barred, and on the door in chalk: ‘Tue – Kordon’. One hatch is frosted on the inside, and in the frost the trace of a finger: a house with a roof and chimney, half wiped away. The frost is old. The wagon has run before.
strings.explore.berlin.ost.porters.title: The porters
strings.explore.berlin.ost.porters.text: Two porters with brass badges on their caps, number 14 and number 31, push their barrows to the through coach for Karsk. Number 14 carries an old woman’s suitcase and takes no money. Number 31 takes double and carries two for it. Between them it evens out, they say. On the corridor platform everyone reckons like that.
strings.explore.berlin.ost.station_clock.title: Twenty thirty-one
strings.explore.berlin.ost.station_clock.text: The station clock hangs under the glass roof in the steam; the minute hand jumps with a jolt: 20:31. An enamel sign beside it: ‘Local time Karsk + 2’. It’s half past ten there now. The corridor trains run by our clock, over there too. I picture Morozov looking at two clocks and taking one of them for wrong.
strings.explore.berlin.ost.ticket_stub.title: A ticket stub
strings.explore.berlin.ost.ticket_stub.text: Between two planks at the end of the platform, a cardboard ticket stub: ‘Berlin Ost – Karsk and return, 2nd class’, punched last autumn. The return half was never used. Either someone over there found what he was looking for, or it found him. I pocket the stub, knowing I ought to throw it away.
strings.explore.berlin.k14.chat_kuhnert.title: Kuhnert in the carriageway
strings.explore.berlin.k14.chat_kuhnert.text: Kuhnert is waiting in the carriageway for the gentlemen, the box under his arm. It’s nothing personal, he says. There has to be order, otherwise someone asks why not.
strings.explore.berlin.k14.chat_kuhnert.l1: Herr Adler, isn’t it? From the building office. Visiting your sister. At this hour.
strings.explore.berlin.k14.chat_kuhnert.l2: You’re standing out here, Herr Kuhnert. In this cold.
strings.explore.berlin.k14.chat_kuhnert.l3: Inspection from ten tonight. The gentlemen come when they come. I have to be here.
strings.explore.berlin.k14.chat_kuhnert.l4: And what do the gentlemen inspect?
strings.explore.berlin.k14.chat_kuhnert.l5: The index. Whether everyone lives where they live. It’s nothing personal, Herr Adler.
strings.explore.berlin.k14.chat_kuhnert.l6: Everything is in order at my sister’s.
strings.explore.berlin.k14.chat_kuhnert.l7: There has to be order, Herr Adler, otherwise someone asks why not.
strings.explore.berlin.k14.basket_rope.title: A basket on a line
strings.explore.berlin.k14.basket_rope.text: From the dark kitchen window on the second floor at the front, a basket hangs on a washing line. Frau Grabowski’s coal card has been blocked since her son went over the Line. Two shovelfuls, says Hanna, nobody will notice.
strings.explore.berlin.k14.basket_rope.l1: Young man! Not so loud. Up here, second floor, front.
strings.explore.berlin.k14.basket_rope.l3: Grabowski. The basket’s for coal. My card’s been blocked since my boy went over the Line.
strings.explore.berlin.k14.basket_rope.l5: Because of order, Herr Kuhnert says. Your sister got briquettes today. Two shovelfuls nobody will notice, she says.
strings.explore.berlin.k14.basket_coal.title: Two shovelfuls
strings.explore.berlin.k14.basket_coal.text: Next to the cellar hatch, Hanna’s briquettes, delivered today, not yet carried down. I take the shovel leaning against the hatch. Two shovelfuls, then a third, because the second was only half. The basket grows heavy. Behind the window of the lodge the curtain doesn’t move. Or it moves in a way I can’t see.
strings.explore.berlin.k14.basket_up.title: Light on the second floor
strings.explore.berlin.k14.basket_up.text: Frau Grabowski has pulled the basket up, three shovelfuls of briquettes. There is a light in her kitchen now. In the dark, she says, you feel the cold less, because you can’t see your breath.
strings.explore.berlin.k14.basket_up.l4: My boy always took one more too. Now I can sit in the kitchen again. I’ll put the light on.
strings.explore.berlin.k14.basket_up.l5: You were sitting in the dark?
strings.explore.berlin.k14.basket_up.l6: In the dark you feel the cold less, because you can’t see your breath. And don’t tell Kuhnert. He counts shovelfuls.
strings.explore.berlin.k14.frozen_laundry.title: Frozen washing
strings.explore.berlin.k14.frozen_laundry.text: Across the yard, lines of washing, frozen stiff: shirts like boards, a sheet that no longer flaps, children’s stockings in three sizes. Tuesday is washing day in the side wing. The drying loft is open and full, so the rest hangs in the yard and freezes. The whole building has done its washing, as if today were a Tuesday like any other.
strings.explore.berlin.k14.chat_hanna.title: Hanna in the yard
strings.explore.berlin.k14.chat_hanna.text: Today Hanna wrote ‘family’ on the blackboard, with a big F. Frau Pohl reports reliably and brings biscuits at Christmas; both are true. I was always the elder. She was always the braver.
strings.explore.berlin.k14.chat_hanna.l1: You’ve got chalk on your sleeve.
strings.explore.berlin.k14.chat_hanna.l2: I always have chalk on my sleeve. Today it was ‘family’ on the board, for the second form. With a big F.
strings.explore.berlin.k14.chat_hanna.l4: Hears everything and reports it reliably. At Christmas she brought me biscuits. Both are true.
strings.explore.berlin.k14.chat_hanna.l6: Then a teacher hid a child. That’s in no curriculum. It’s in every fairy tale.
strings.explore.berlin.k14.chat_hanna.l7: You were always the braver one.
strings.explore.berlin.k14.chat_hanna.l8: I was always the younger one – she’s allowed. Go on, Mr Architect. Find your way.
strings.explore.berlin.k14.ilse_drawing.title: A house in the frost
strings.explore.berlin.k14.ilse_drawing.text: In the pane of the stairwell door, painted into the frost from the inside with a child’s finger: a house with five storeys, all windows lit, even those in the cellar. At the top a curl of smoke, at the bottom a door standing open. Ilse was here. I breathe on the glass until the lines blur. Kuhnert is not to read houses.
strings.explore.berlin.k14.cellar_hatch.title: The cellar hatch
strings.explore.berlin.k14.cellar_hatch.text: The cellar hatch is open, an iron flap in the paving, beneath it the chute for the coal. Down below a passage runs under all three wings, front building, side wing, rear building. In the war that was the air-raid route; there are still arrows in luminous paint on the walls. Whoever goes into the cellar today is fetching coal. Whoever goes through at night wants to come out somewhere else.
strings.explore.berlin.k14.windows.title: Nothing but windows
strings.explore.berlin.k14.windows.text: From the yard, the building is a calendar of windows. Here a radio and a desk lamp, there a baby that won’t sleep, in the rear building a kitchen where cards are being played. In the side wing a curtain that moves as soon as I stop. Three windows sealed with strips of paper. In Kuhnert’s box each is a card. On my plans each was a rectangle.
strings.explore.berlin.k14.dustbins.title: The dustbins
strings.explore.berlin.k14.dustbins.text: Four dustbins under caps of snow, each marked with its part of the building and number in white paint. Fir branches stick out of the front building’s, still from Christmas, a chair leg out of the rear building’s. The bin ‘RB 3’ is empty and clean, lined with newspaper. Nobody has thrown anything away there since October. ‘Relocated’, my files call that.
strings.explore.berlin.k14.carpet_rack.title: The carpet rail
strings.explore.berlin.k14.carpet_rack.text: The carpet-beating rail in the middle of the yard, iron, with an enamel sign: ‘Beating on weekdays only, 08:00–12:00 and 15:00–18:00. The House Rules.’ Beneath it, the chalk lines of a hopscotch game, half under snow. Hanna and I did gymnastics on a rail like this as children, in another yard. In Berlin all the yards have the same rail and the same rules.
strings.explore.berlin.k14.workshop_window.title: Shoes with names
strings.explore.berlin.k14.workshop_window.text: The basement windows of Pietsch’s shoe repair, half below the paving. Inside, on shelves, the shoes of the whole building, a slip on every pair: Mertens, Kühn, Lenz, Schulz, two small pairs Mertens. Pietsch keeps the only index in the building that nobody reads: he knows how everyone walks. On his door it says ‘Commercial premises’. No household card, no household.
strings.task.berlin.basket.title: A basket for Frau Grabowski
strings.task.berlin.basket.summary: A basket hangs on a line from a dark window in the front building. Frau Grabowski’s coal card has been blocked since her son went over the Line.
strings.task.berlin.basket.hint.rope: Under the dark kitchen window in the front building, a basket hangs on a line.
strings.task.berlin.basket.hint.coal: Hanna’s briquettes are next to the cellar hatch. Two shovelfuls, Frau Grabowski said.
strings.task.berlin.basket.hint.up: Take the full basket back under her window.
strings.mg.turntable.title: The turntable
strings.mg.turntable.subtitle: The press minder wants the sooty Kukushka out of the picture before the Swede arrives. Grigori, who usually works the turntable, is playing the tuba today.
strings.mg.turntable.instruction: Turn the bridge to stall 7, brake it to a stop and only move the engine on when the rails line up in the magnifier.
strings.mg.turntable.status.start: The bridge is at the approach. Stall 7 is top left.
strings.mg.turntable.status.turning: The bridge is turning, {speed} degrees per second.
strings.mg.turntable.status.coasting: The bridge is coasting, {speed} degrees per second.
strings.mg.turntable.fail.moving: The bridge is still moving. The engine jerks forward, the buffers bang, it rolls back.
strings.mg.turntable.fail.gap: The wheels strike the rail edge, {cm} out. The engine rolls back.
strings.mg.turntable.fail.between: Between the tracks the engine finds no rail. It jerks, the buffers bang, it stops.
strings.mg.turntable.fail.wrong: The rails line up, but this is stall {n}. The Kukushka belongs in stall 7.
strings.mg.turntable.fail.entry: That’s the approach. It has just come from there.
strings.mg.turntable.solved: The bolt drops in, the rails line up. The Kukushka rolls into stall 7, the door closes. Now the Swede sees only the model engine.
strings.mg.turntable.hint.1: The bridge coasts a long way. Let go early, brake with the space bar and set the last few centimetres with short nudges.
strings.mg.turntable.hint.next: Stall 7 is at {deg}° on the index circle; the bridge is at {now}°. Brake about ten degrees before and only move on when the magnifier shows ‘aligned’.
strings.mg.turntable.side.head: Index circle
strings.mg.turntable.side.note: With the engine on it, the bridge weighs over a hundred tonnes. What has started turning keeps turning.
strings.mg.luggage.title: The luggage scale
strings.mg.luggage.subtitle: The official only stamps what has been weighed, and the family can’t manage the decimal scale. The D 303 to Karsk leaves at ten past nine.
strings.mg.luggage.instruction: Slide the weights until the pointer settles on the mark, then take the reading. The corridor allows 20 kg per suitcase and 5 kg per parcel.
strings.mg.luggage.status.up: The pointer is high: too little weight on the beam.
strings.mg.luggage.status.down: The pointer is low: too much weight on the beam.
strings.mg.luggage.status.near: Almost. The pointer trembles close to the mark.
strings.mg.luggage.status.level: The pointer settles. Take the reading now.
strings.mg.luggage.fail: Reading: {read}. But the pointer is {dir}; the official shakes his head.
strings.mg.luggage.result.1: 23.6 kg, three kilos six hundred too much. The mother repacks coffee, oranges and a tin of ham into a parcel.
strings.mg.luggage.result.2: 19.8 kg. The official nods and stamps the suitcase.
strings.mg.luggage.result.3: 3.8 kg. A parcel up to five kilos may go. Stamp.
strings.mg.luggage.solved: Suitcase 19.8 kg, parcel 3.8 kg. Everything may go, just in two pieces.
strings.mg.luggage.hint.1: Coarse first: the big weight in the last notch where the pointer still stays high. Then the small one until it settles.
strings.mg.luggage.hint.next: Big weight at {coarse} kg, then slide the small one to {fine} kg.
strings.mg.luggage.slip.head: Luggage ticket D 303
strings.mg.luggage.beam.coarse: Large sliding weight: 5 kg per notch
strings.mg.luggage.beam.fine: Small sliding weight: 0.1 kg per mark
strings.mg.luggage.sign.2: Suitcases up to 20 kg each · Parcels up to 5 kg
